While memorability bins were fixed by these sequences, the particular images assigned to each trial were randomized for each participant.

Then, regardless of whether the recognition judgment was correct, the old card was shown alone and participants had 2 seconds to make a 2-alternativeforced-choice value memory report, between $0 and $1.

Second, during the choice phase, participants had 3 seconds to choose between two previously-rated food items (using a computer keyboard), imagining they would eat a snack-sized portion of the selected food item.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Cue Memorability Drives Associative Retrieval of Value
table.research_questions:
1. Are more memorable images better cues for retrieving associated values? That is, are people’s choices more sensitive to associated values when a cue image is more memorable? (Experiments 1,2,3,4)
2. Are more memorable images more likely to be chosen, regardless of their associated value? (Experiments 1,4)
3. Does cue memorability influence value-based choices even in the domain of food choices, where preferences are subjective, choice options are highly familiar, and values are associated with categories rather than specific image cues? (Experiment 5)

These research questions and corresponding hypotheses are operationalized in the different experiments as follows (see “Statistical Models” for exact model specifications):

Experiment 1
H1.1 Participants will make more accurate choices for more memorable old cards, reflecting stronger retrieval of the card’s associated value — i.e., an interaction between memorability and value in predicting old-card choice. 
H1.2: Participants will be overall more likely to choose old cards with more memorable images, independent of their associated value. 

Experiment 2
H2.1: Recognition memory (correctly identifying which of the two cards was seen before) will be more accurate for more memorable images. 
H2.2: Explicit value recall (correctly reporting whether an old card was worth $0 or $1) will be more accurate for more memorable images. This finding would rule out a recognition-driven account of the effects and provide unambiguous support for stronger associative memory for the value of more memorable images.

Experiment 3
H3.1: Participants will make more accurate (higher-expected-value) choices between two previously-seen cards when both cards are high-memorability than when both are low-memorability, consistent with H1.1.
H3.2: Alternatively, if memorability does not interact with value, there should be no difference between these two conditions.
(“even” trials) 

Experiment 4
H4.1: When two old cards have the same value, participants will be more likely to select the high-memorability card when both are $1, and more likely to select the low-memorability card when both are $0 (i.e., interaction between overall value and memorability on choice). This would indicate that participants are more strongly influenced by their memory for the memorable image’s value, rather than an overall bias towards choosing the memorable image.
H4.2: Alternately, participants will be more likely to choose the higher memorability card, regardless of image value.
 
Experiment 5
H5.1: Even in food choices, where value associations have been learned over many experiences, more memorable images (i.e. the memorability of both images) result in decisions that are more consistent with reported values. This predicts an interaction between value difference and overall memorability.
H5.2: When both options have similar high values, participants are more likely to choose the more memorable image but when both options have similar low values, participants are more likely to choose the less memorable image (interaction between memorability and overall value).
H5.3: When both options have the same value, participants are more likely to choose the more memorable image (i.e. overall memorability bias, in contrast to H5.2).

Eligibility requirements include currently residing in the United States and speaking English as a first language. table.sample_size_rationale:
This sample size is a conservative estimate determined by our pilot experiments. For completeness, we include a power analysis below for our main analysis of interest, H1.2, on the interaction of memorability with value on old trial choices in Experiment 1.

We determined sample size via a parametric-bootstrap power analysis targeting our primary hypothesis: the interaction between memorability and value in predicting old-card choice in Experiment 1 (H1.1). We fit the confirmatory generalized linear mixed-effects model to Experiment 1's pilot data (n=106 included participants, 16,253 old-trial observations), then used the fitted model's estimated fixed effects and random-effect variances as data-generating parameters to simulate new datasets under the same design. For each of several candidate sample sizes, we randomly subsampled that many participants' worth of simulated data, refit the model, and recorded whether the interaction term reached significance (p < .05, two-tailed); this was repeated 150 times per candidate N. Power exceeded 80% between N=20 and N=30, and plateaued near 99–100% by N=50–60. We selected N=100 per experiment—well above the ~80%-power threshold—for conservativeness, and to match sample sizes in other studies in the literature.
table.stopping_rule: Recruitment will continue for each experiment until the post-exclusion included sample size reaches the target size (see “Sample Size” above).

table.transformations: For modeling purposes, we will center old values so that a value of 0 is transformed to -1. Memorability bins enter models either as an ordered 2 or 3-level factor (low < mid < high) with polynomial contrasts. In the 2-level case, this is equivalent to a centered linear coding where low = -1 and high = 1.

table.data_exclusion_criteria:
We will exclude participants who meet any of the following criteria:
Failed or responded incorrectly to any of 3 attention check trials (including responses that match hidden-text prompt designed to identify AI-agents)
Non-response rate of above 20% of trials
Failure to reliably learn associations between images and values. We will conduct a binomial test to determine if overall subject accuracy is significantly above chance (50%), which is unbiased with respect to the hypothesized analyses of memorability.
table.missing_data_handling: Choice trials will end if subjects fail to respond within two seconds. We will exclude those trials from further analysis. If a participant does not complete the whole experiment, all their data is excluded.
table.study_design_overview:
All five experiments are within-subject repeated-measures designs implemented as self-paced, single-session online tasks (jsPsych, data collected via Prolific). In the first four experiments, every participant is assigned a full trial sequence drawn from a small set of pre-computed sequences (see below); the only participant-to-participant randomization is (a) which of these pre-computed trial sequences they receive, (b) which specific images from the memorability-binned stimulus pool are assigned to which trial slot, and (c) left/right screen placement. There are no between-subjects conditions of interest.

Stimulus Set (Experiments 1-4)
Stimuli are drawn from the THINGS image database (Hebart et al. 2019) using THINGS memorability scores (memorability_cr, the corrected-recognition memorability score; Kramer et al., 2023). “THINGS is a hierarchically structured dataset containing 26,107 images representing 1854 object concepts (such as aardvark, tank, and zucchini)..., 1619 of which are assigned to 27 higher categories (such as animal, weapon, and food)” (Kramer et al., 2023). 
We use images from the 26 higher categories that have at least 6 object concepts (excluding “insects”). From those, we choose six images from each higher category, two in each of three memorability bins (low, medium and high). We use mixed integer linear programming (MILP) to choose images that maximize the difference in memorability between these bins under the constraint that no two images are of the same object concept. This results in 26 × 3 × 6 = 468 images total (156 per bin). Specifically, the low bin is selected to minimize memorability score, the high bin to maximize it, and the mid bin to minimize |score − sample median|. 

In the resulting set, mean (range) memorability_cr by bin is: low = 0.550 (0.410–0.692), mid = 0.795 (0.789–0.805), high = 0.952 (0.881–1.000). Experiments 1 & 2 use all 468 images from all 3 bins, whereas experiments 3 & 4 use only the low and high bins.

Sequence pre-computation (Experiments 1-4)
The trial-level structure (old/new status, memorability bin, delay, value, and — where applicable — cross-condition pairing) is fixed in advance by the MILP solver. Ten independent MILP solutions are pre-computed per experiment (Experiment 2 uses the exact same sequences as Experiment 1); a participant is assigned one of the ten deterministically via a hash of their participant ID, so that participants are spread roughly evenly across the ten available sequences. The purpose of this design is to strictly control for possible interactions between the variables of interest and potential confounds. Details of which variables are balanced for which tasks are included below.

Additional design details for each experiment are described below:

Experiment 1
In experiment 1, we test whether image memorability drives stronger memory for associated values. To do so, we implement the card game described in Duncan & Shohamy (2016), dropping the contextual cues from the original design. The task consists of 312 trials, and includes all 468 selected stimulus images. Half of trials (156) are “new,” consisting of two novel cards, in which the chosen one flips over to reveal its value. The other half (156) are “old” trials, in which the participant chooses between a previously chosen card and a novel foil (and once again receives feedback). The delay between a new trial and its subsequent old trial is 7-15 trials. On all trials, both images presented are of the same memorability bin. Accurate choices on old trials are defined as choosing $1 cards or avoiding $0 cards (i.e., choosing the novel card). 

The full trial structure is solved offline by a two-phase MILP. The distributions of delays are precisely matched across memorability bins and old card values; left/right position of the old card is also balanced within participants. To limit large strings of consecutive trials of the same memorability bin or trial type, no more than 3 consecutive same-memorability trials can occur in a row, nor more than 8 consecutive old or new trials (to accommodate the first 7 trials which must be new).  

Each choice trial consists of up to 2 seconds to respond (using the ‘j’ and ‘k’ keys), followed by a 1-second highlight of the chosen card. It then flips over and reveals its value ($0 or $1) for 1.5 seconds. A “too slow” message appears if no choice is made, and a randomly selected card flips over. The inter-trial interval is 0.5 seconds. Three attention checks are interspersed in the trial sequence. Participants are paid a performance-dependent bonus; 10 old-card trials are sampled at random at the end of the session and their outcomes summed, normalized by the maximum possible ($10), and scaled to a $2 maximum bonus on top of a $5 base payment for an estimated 25-minute session.

We test for an overall bias of memorability on choice (are participants more likely to choose more memorable old cards?), and based on our hypotheses, an interaction between memorability and value (are participants more likely to make accurate choices for more memorable old cards?). See “Research Questions” section above for more details and hypotheses.

Experiment 2
In experiment 2, we isolate recognition memory from associative (value) memory, which are conflated within a single choice on experiment 1's old trials. This experiment reuses experiment 1's exact trial sequences and stimulus set (312 trials, all three memorability bins, the same 10 pre-computed sequences), changing only what happens on old trials. New trials are unchanged. On old trials, participants first make a forced-choice recognition judgment (“which of these two cards have you seen before?”, up to 2s), see feedback via a colored highlight (green if correct, red if incorrect, 0.75s) — and then, regardless of whether the recognition judgment was correct, report the old card's value from memory ($0/$1, up to 2s, 0.75s feedback), with the two response keys fixed to left/right screen position rather than tied to the recognition choice or the old card's actual side.

The bonus on this task is accuracy-based rather than reward-based: overall accuracy across all recognition and value-report trials is pooled, chance-adjusted (0.5 subtracted and rescaled to 0–1), and scaled to a $2 maximum bonus on top of a $4 base payment, for an estimated 20-minute session. We test whether recognition accuracy is higher for more memorable images, and whether value-report accuracy is higher for more memorable images — including restricted to trials where the card was correctly recognized, to rule out recognition itself as the driver. See “Research Questions” above for hypotheses.

Experiment 3
In experiment 3, we test whether the interaction between memorability and value found in experiment 1 is still present when deciding between two old cards (independent of the novel foil card in experiment 1). To do so, we modify the old trials so that both cards have previously been chosen and are now equally familiar: participants choose between two previously-seen cards, one whose source trial was worth $1 and one whose source trial was worth $0. Accurate choices are defined as choosing the $1 card. Both cards on an old trial are always from the same memorability bin, so a bias toward the more memorable card cannot by itself produce a correct answer. For analytical simplicity, we restrict this experiment to the high and low memorability bins (dropping mid); each bin's 156 images are consumed exactly once per participant.

The task consists of 234 trials: 156 “new” encoding trials (78 high-memorability pairs, 78 low-memorability pairs, each split 39 $1 / 39 $0) and 78 “old” trials (39 high-memorability pairs, 39 low-memorability pairs). Because each old trial draws on two previously-chosen cards rather than one, every new trial's chosen card is later reused as a source (156 new trials ÷ 2 sources per old trial = 78 old trials, with no leftover sources). As in experiment 1, delay (7–15 trials) is matched across memorability bins and value conditions, left/right position and which side carries the longer delay are balanced within participants, and the same run-length caps apply (no more than 3 consecutive same-bin trials, no more than 8 consecutive same-type trials).

Trial timing, attention checks, and the bonus mechanism are identical to experiment 1, scaled to an estimated 20-minute session with a $4 base payment and $2 maximum bonus. We test for an interaction of memorability and value — are participants more likely to make accurate choices on high-memorability trials than low-memorability trials? See “Research Questions” above for hypotheses.

Experiment 4
In experiment 4, we test how memorability influences choice when the two options' values are similar or equal, rather than always favoring one clear answer. This offers the cleanest test of the overall “memorability bias” —are participants more likely to choose the memorable image, when values are exactly matched? Or alternatively, is choice bias modulated by value—choosing the more memorable card when both are $1, and choosing the less memorable card when both are $0 (consistent with making a choice preferentially weighted by the retrieved value of the memorable card). As in experiment 2, we restrict images to the high and low memorability bins and old trials pit two previously-chosen cards against each other, but here the two cards are always drawn from different bins — one high-memorability source and one low-memorability source. Old trials fall into four types: two “even” types where both cards share the same value (both $1 or both $0), and two “uneven” types where one card is $1 and the other $0 (i.e., there is a correct answer).

The task consists of 234 trials: 156 new encoding trials (78 high-memorability, 78 low-memorability, each split 39 $1 and 39 $0) and 78 old trials—40 “even” (20 both $0, 20 both $1) and 38 “uneven” (19 high = $1, low = $0; 19 high = $0, low = $1). Delay distributions are matched separately within the even and uneven groups so that the high- and low-memorability bins end up with identical overall delay distributions; the high-memorability source has the longer delay on exactly half of the uneven trials and half of the even trials. The same run-length caps as experiments 1–2 apply. Trial timing, the bonus mechanism, session length/pay, and the fixed attention-check positions match experiment 2.

On even trials, we test whether participants are biased toward choosing the more memorable card overall, and whether that bias is modulated by value (e.g., toward the memorable card when both are worth $1, away from it when both are worth $0). The main purpose of the uneven trials is so participants cannot predict that all old trials have no optimal choice and must engage in memory retrieval consistently, although we do not have strong hypotheses about performance. See “Research Questions” above.

Experiment 5
We replicate the sequential food-choice paradigm from Li et al. (2025) to test for our hypothesized interactions (see H5.1/H5.2 under “Research Questions” above). We will leverage the memorability scores estimated in Experiment 1A of Li et al. in our design and analysis. We will follow the design of Experiment 1B in which subjects first complete a rating phase (where they rate each food option) followed by a choice phase (where they choose between two food options). In order to more cleanly test our hypotheses about memorability, we will use only a portion of the 138 images used in Li et al. (2022). We will split the image set into terciles by measured memorability scores, and only use images in the lowest and highest terciles. This will produce a final stimulus set of 92 images: 46 high-memorability and 46 low-memorability.

In choosing the pairing of options, Li et al. (2022) designed two trial types. In similar value trials, we will follow exactly the pairing procedure of Li et al. (2022): all 92 images will be ranked by a participant's reported preferences, and adjacent ranks will be paired to be displayed together on choice trials. This procedure ignores memorability, but will likely produce similar-value trials both across- and within-memorability bin. These similar-value trials (akin to "even trials" in Experiment 4) will test for an interaction between the overall value and difference in memorability.

In distant value trials, Li et al. (2022) paired each ranked image with one at a fixed interval away (e.g., image 1 with image 70, image 2 with image 71, etc.). We will follow the same procedure, but only within each memorability bin (e.g., high-mem image 1 with high-mem image 23, high-mem image 2 with high-mem image 24; low-mem image 1 with low-mem image 23, low-mem image 2 with low-mem image 24). These distant value trials will test for an interaction between overall memorability and difference in value.

Experiment 5a
The design of experiment 5a is the same as experiment 5 with one small change to the distant-value condition. In the distant-value condition, we pair each ranked image (within memorability bin) with another one at a fixed interval away. In 5a, we use an interval of 8 rather than 23 (as above), in order to make choices slightly less consistent, while still having an option that is systematically preferred. We believe this will allow sufficient variability in these choices in order to properly test for an interaction with memorability.
table.sample_size:
Each experiment 1-5 will sample 100 post-exclusion participants (see inclusion criteria below). Because of our within-subject design, all analyses are balanced across all 100 participants.

Experiment 5a will sample 500 post-exclusion participants in order to increase precision in this more naturalistic experiment.
table.statistical_tests:
We will fit these models using the glmer function in lme4. For models that do not converge, we will follow the algorithm from Bates et al. (2015) to find the maximal model that converges. We will then follow Bates in using likelihood ratio tests to select an appropriate model.

Experiment 1:
old_value: centered value of old option (1 if value = $1, -1 if value = $0)
memorabilty_bin: low, medium, high (orthogonal polynomial contrasts)
old_image: ID of old image 
new_image: ID of new image

glmer(chose_old ~ old_value * memorability_bin + 
              (old_value * memorability_bin | participant_id) + (old_value | old_image) + (1 | new_image), family = binomial)

Experiment 2:
old_value: centered value of old option (1 if value = $1, -1 if value = $0)
memorabilty_bin: low, medium, high (orthogonal polynomial contrasts)
old_image: ID of old image 
new_image: ID of new image

glmer(correct_recognition ~ old_value * memorability_bin + 
              (old_value * memorability_bin | participant_id) + (old_value | old_image) + (1 | new_image), family = binomial)
glmer(correct_recall ~ old_value * memorability_bin + 
              (old_value * memorability_bin | participant_id) + (old_value | old_image) + (1 | new_image), family = binomial)

Experiment 3:
memorability_bin: 1 if high, -1 if low
high_image: ID of image associated with high value
low_image: ID of image associated with low value
glmer(correct ~ memorability_bin + 
              (memorability_bin | participant_id) + (1 | high_image) + (1 | low_image), 
            family = binomial)

Experiment 4:
high_mem_value: 1 if high memorability image associated with $1, -1 if high memorability image associated with $0
high_mem_image: ID of high memorability image 
low_mem_image: ID of low memorability image
glmer(chose_high_mem ~ overall_value + 
              (overall_value | participant_id) + (overall_value | high_mem_image) + (overall_value | low_mem_image), 
            family = binomial)

Experiment 5:
Values will be z-scored within participant.
chose_right: chose option on right
delta_value: right option value - left option value
overall_value: right option value + left option value
delta_memorability: right image memorability  - left image memorability
overall_memorability: right image memorability + left image memorability

We will first fit models separately by trial type (similar-value and distant-value). On similar value trials, we will fit:

glmer(chose_right ~ delta_memorability * overall_value +
(delta_memorability * overall_value | participant_id) + (1 | right_image) + (1 | left_image), family = binomial)

And on distant value trials, we will fit:
glmer(chose_right ~ delta_value * overall_memorability +
(delta_value * overall_memorability | participant_id) + (1 | right_image) + (1 | left_image), family = binomial)

Finally, we will fit the following model on the entire dataset:

glmer(chose_right ~ delta_value * overall_memorability + delta_memorability * overall_value +
(delta_value * overall_memorability + delta_memorability * overall_value | participant_id) + (1 | right_image) + (1 | left_image), family = binomial)

Experiment 5a:
Analysis will use the same approach as Experiment 5.

If a participant does not complete the whole experiment, all their data is excluded.", "All five experiments are within-subject repeated-measures designs implemented as self-paced, single-session online tasks (jsPsych, data collected via Prolific). In the first four experiments, every participant is assigned a full trial sequence drawn from a small set of pre-computed sequences (see below); the only participant-to-participant randomization is (a) which of these pre-computed trial sequences they receive, (b) which specific images from the memorability-binned stimulus pool are assigned to which trial slot, and (c) left/right screen placement. There are no between-subjects conditions of interest.

Stimulus Set (Experiments 1-4)
Stimuli are drawn from the THINGS image database (Hebart et al. 2019) using THINGS memorability scores (memorability_cr, the corrected-recognition memorability score; Kramer et al., 2023). “THINGS is a hierarchically structured dataset containing 26,107 images representing 1854 object concepts (such as aardvark, tank, and zucchini)..., 1619 of which are assigned to 27 higher categories (such as animal, weapon, and food)” (Kramer et al., 2023).
We use images from the 26 higher categories that have at least 6 object concepts (excluding “insects”). From those, we choose six images from each higher category, two in each of three memorability bins (low, medium and high). We use mixed integer linear programming (MILP) to choose images that maximize the difference in memorability between these bins under the constraint that no two images are of the same object concept. This results in 26 × 3 × 6 = 468 images total (156 per bin). Specifically, the low bin is selected to minimize memorability score, the high bin to maximize it, and the mid bin to minimize |score − sample median|.

In the resulting set, mean (range) memorability_cr by bin is: low = 0.550 (0.410–0.692), mid = 0.795 (0.789–0.805), high = 0.952 (0.881–1.000). Experiments 1 & 2 use all 468 images from all 3 bins, whereas experiments 3 & 4 use only the low and high bins.

Sequence pre-computation (Experiments 1-4)
The trial-level structure (old/new status, memorability bin, delay, value, and — where applicable — cross-condition pairing) is fixed in advance by the MILP solver. Ten independent MILP solutions are pre-computed per experiment (Experiment 2 uses the exact same sequences as Experiment 1); a participant is assigned one of the ten deterministically via a hash of their participant ID, so that participants are spread roughly evenly across the ten available sequences. The purpose of this design is to strictly control for possible interactions between the variables of interest and potential confounds. Details of which variables are balanced for which tasks are included below.

Additional design details for each experiment are described below:

Experiment 1
In experiment 1, we test whether image memorability drives stronger memory for associated values. To do so, we implement the card game described in Duncan & Shohamy (2016), dropping the contextual cues from the original design. The task consists of 312 trials, and includes all 468 selected stimulus images. Half of trials (156) are “new,” consisting of two novel cards, in which the chosen one flips over to reveal its value. The other half (156) are “old” trials, in which the participant chooses between a previously chosen card and a novel foil (and once again receives feedback). The delay between a new trial and its subsequent old trial is 7-15 trials. On all trials, both images presented are of the same memorability bin. Accurate choices on old trials are defined as choosing $1 cards or avoiding $0 cards (i.e., choosing the novel card).

The full trial structure is solved offline by a two-phase MILP. The distributions of delays are precisely matched across memorability bins and old card values; left/right position of the old card is also balanced within participants. To limit large strings of consecutive trials of the same memorability bin or trial type, no more than 3 consecutive same-memorability trials can occur in a row, nor more than 8 consecutive old or new trials (to accommodate the first 7 trials which must be new).

Each choice trial consists of up to 2 seconds to respond (using the ‘j’ and ‘k’ keys), followed by a 1-second highlight of the chosen card. It then flips over and reveals its value ($0 or $1) for 1.5 seconds. A “too slow” message appears if no choice is made, and a randomly selected card flips over. The inter-trial interval is 0.5 seconds. Three attention checks are interspersed in the trial sequence. Participants are paid a performance-dependent bonus; 10 old-card trials are sampled at random at the end of the session and their outcomes summed, normalized by the maximum possible ($10), and scaled to a $2 maximum bonus on top of a $5 base payment for an estimated 25-minute session.

We test for an overall bias of memorability on choice (are participants more likely to choose more memorable old cards?), and based on our hypotheses, an interaction between memorability and value (are participants more likely to make accurate choices for more memorable old cards?). See “Research Questions” section above for more details and hypotheses.

Experiment 2
In experiment 2, we isolate recognition memory from associative (value) memory, which are conflated within a single choice on experiment 1's old trials. This experiment reuses experiment 1's exact trial sequences and stimulus set (312 trials, all three memorability bins, the same 10 pre-computed sequences), changing only what happens on old trials. New trials are unchanged. On old trials, participants first make a forced-choice recognition judgment (“which of these two cards have you seen before?”, up to 2s), see feedback via a colored highlight (green if correct, red if incorrect, 0.75s) — and then, regardless of whether the recognition judgment was correct, report the old card's value from memory ($0/$1, up to 2s, 0.75s feedback), with the two response keys fixed to left/right screen position rather than tied to the recognition choice or the old card's actual side.

The bonus on this task is accuracy-based rather than reward-based: overall accuracy across all recognition and value-report trials is pooled, chance-adjusted (0.5 subtracted and rescaled to 0–1), and scaled to a $2 maximum bonus on top of a $4 base payment, for an estimated 20-minute session. We test whether recognition accuracy is higher for more memorable images, and whether value-report accuracy is higher for more memorable images — including restricted to trials where the card was correctly recognized, to rule out recognition itself as the driver. See “Research Questions” above for hypotheses.

Experiment 3
In experiment 3, we test whether the interaction between memorability and value found in experiment 1 is still present when deciding between two old cards (independent of the novel foil card in experiment 1). To do so, we modify the old trials so that both cards have previously been chosen and are now equally familiar: participants choose between two previously-seen cards, one whose source trial was worth $1 and one whose source trial was worth $0. Accurate choices are defined as choosing the $1 card. Both cards on an old trial are always from the same memorability bin, so a bias toward the more memorable card cannot by itself produce a correct answer. For analytical simplicity, we restrict this experiment to the high and low memorability bins (dropping mid); each bin's 156 images are consumed exactly once per participant.

The task consists of 234 trials: 156 “new” encoding trials (78 high-memorability pairs, 78 low-memorability pairs, each split 39 $1 / 39 $0) and 78 “old” trials (39 high-memorability pairs, 39 low-memorability pairs). Because each old trial draws on two previously-chosen cards rather than one, every new trial's chosen card is later reused as a source (156 new trials ÷ 2 sources per old trial = 78 old trials, with no leftover sources). As in experiment 1, delay (7–15 trials) is matched across memorability bins and value conditions, left/right position and which side carries the longer delay are balanced within participants, and the same run-length caps apply (no more than 3 consecutive same-bin trials, no more than 8 consecutive same-type trials).

Trial timing, attention checks, and the bonus mechanism are identical to experiment 1, scaled to an estimated 20-minute session with a $4 base payment and $2 maximum bonus. We test for an interaction of memorability and value — are participants more likely to make accurate choices on high-memorability trials than low-memorability trials? See “Research Questions” above for hypotheses.

Experiment 4
In experiment 4, we test how memorability influences choice when the two options' values are similar or equal, rather than always favoring one clear answer. This offers the cleanest test of the overall “memorability bias” —are participants more likely to choose the memorable image, when values are exactly matched? Or alternatively, is choice bias modulated by value—choosing the more memorable card when both are $1, and choosing the less memorable card when both are $0 (consistent with making a choice preferentially weighted by the retrieved value of the memorable card). As in experiment 2, we restrict images to the high and low memorability bins and old trials pit two previously-chosen cards against each other, but here the two cards are always drawn from different bins — one high-memorability source and one low-memorability source. Old trials fall into four types: two “even” types where both cards share the same value (both $1 or both $0), and two “uneven” types where one card is $1 and the other $0 (i.e., there is a correct answer).

The task consists of 234 trials: 156 new encoding trials (78 high-memorability, 78 low-memorability, each split 39 $1 and 39 $0) and 78 old trials—40 “even” (20 both $0, 20 both $1) and 38 “uneven” (19 high = $1, low = $0; 19 high = $0, low = $1). Delay distributions are matched separately within the even and uneven groups so that the high- and low-memorability bins end up with identical overall delay distributions; the high-memorability source has the longer delay on exactly half of the uneven trials and half of the even trials. The same run-length caps as experiments 1–2 apply. Trial timing, the bonus mechanism, session length/pay, and the fixed attention-check positions match experiment 2.

On even trials, we test whether participants are biased toward choosing the more memorable card overall, and whether that bias is modulated by value (e.g., toward the memorable card when both are worth $1, away from it when both are worth $0). The main purpose of the uneven trials is so participants cannot predict that all old trials have no optimal choice and must engage in memory retrieval consistently, although we do not have strong hypotheses about performance. See “Research Questions” above.

Experiment 5
We replicate the sequential food-choice paradigm from Li et al. (2025) to test for our hypothesized interactions (see H5.1/H5.2 under “Research Questions” above). We will leverage the memorability scores estimated in Experiment 1A of Li et al. in our design and analysis. We will follow the design of Experiment 1B in which subjects first complete a rating phase (where they rate each food option) followed by a choice phase (where they choose between two food options). In order to more cleanly test our hypotheses about memorability, we will use only a portion of the 138 images used in Li et al. (2022). We will split the image set into terciles by measured memorability scores, and only use images in the lowest and highest terciles. This will produce a final stimulus set of 92 images: 46 high-memorability and 46 low-memorability.

In choosing the pairing of options, Li et al. (2022) designed two trial types. In similar value trials, we will follow exactly the pairing procedure of Li et al. (2022): all 92 images will be ranked by a participant's reported preferences, and adjacent ranks will be paired to be displayed together on choice trials. This procedure ignores memorability, but will likely produce similar-value trials both across- and within-memorability bin. These similar-value trials (akin to \"even trials\" in Experiment 4) will test for an interaction between the overall value and difference in memorability.

In distant value trials, Li et al. (2022) paired each ranked image with one at a fixed interval away (e.g., image 1 with image 70, image 2 with image 71, etc.). We will follow the same procedure, but only within each memorability bin (e.g., high-mem image 1 with high-mem image 23, high-mem image 2 with high-mem image 24; low-mem image 1 with low-mem image 23, low-mem image 2 with low-mem image 24). These distant value trials will test for an interaction between overall memorability and difference in value.

Experiment 5a
The design of experiment 5a is the same as experiment 5 with one small change to the distant-value condition. In the distant-value condition, we pair each ranked image (within memorability bin) with another one at a fixed interval away. In 5a, we use an interval of 8 rather than 23 (as above), in order to make choices slightly less consistent, while still having an option that is systematically preferred. We believe this will allow sufficient variability in these choices in order to properly test for an interaction with memorability.", "Each experiment 1-5 will sample 100 post-exclusion participants (see inclusion criteria below). report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. ownership.dep_description: When confronted with a decision, we frequently use memory to infer the value of choice options. However, little is known about how the perceptual features of the options themselves influence our ability to successfully retrieve associated value information from memory to guide choices. Here, we test whether image memorability—the population-level likelihood of recognizing a particular visual stimulus during a recognition memory task—influences choices during a memory-guided decision-making task. Across five behavioral experiments, we aim to evaluate if more memorable image cues produce stronger memory traces for associated value, and if these traces are more readily and effectively remembered to guide value-based decisions. For four preregistered experiments, we adapt a version of the memory-guided decision-making task from Duncan Shohamy (2016). live_data_statements: First, we confirmed that our participants were able to successfully learn cue-value associations in this task, replicating previous work (Duncan and Shohamy, 2016).

We found strong evidence for this (linear) interaction between memorability and value (β = .2, SE = .04, p < .001); participants are more likely to choose $1 cards and avoid $0 cards when they are more memorable.
However, on old trials, participants were now instructed to select which card they had previously seen (recognition memory; Fig. 1).

We also found a significant relationship between value and correct recall, such that participants were more likely to correctly recall a $1 association than a $0 association (β = .27, SE = .03, p < .001).
We note that this interaction is supported by the results of Experiment 1, but there participants had to infer the expected value of a novel foil.

On matched-value trials, we found a reliable effect of overall (shared) value on the probability of choosing the higher memorability card (β = 0.26, SE = 0.04, p < .001); consistent with P2, participants were more likely to choose the more memorable card when both were $1 and more likely to choose the less memorable card when both were $0 (Fig. 3B).

In their initial analysis, Li et al. (2022) reported no evidence for an overall memorability bias, consistent with our theoretical and empirical results above; participants were not more likely, overall, to choose foods cued with more memorable images.
This result held even on a subset of trials pairing two foods for which a participant gave similar preference ratings.
We recruited five independent samples of online participants via Prolific.

Eligibility was restricted to Prolific users residing in the United States who reported English as their first language and had an approval rating of at least 99% on previous Prolific studies across at least 50 previous submissions.
All participants provided informed consent, and all procedures were approved by the Columbia University Institutional Review Board.
We applied preregistered exclusion criteria to each sample (see Inclusion Criteria), with a final sample size of N = 100 participants per experiment.
On "new" (encoding) trials, both cards depicted images the participant had not yet seen, and the participant learned the value of the card they chose.
While memorability bins were fixed by these sequences, the particular images assigned to each trial were randomized for each participant.

Then, regardless of whether the recognition judgment was correct, the old card was shown alone and participants had 2 seconds to make a 2-alternativeforced-choice value memory report, between $0 and $1.

Second, during the choice phase, participants had 3 seconds to choose between two previously-rated food items (using a computer keyboard), imagining they would eat a snack-sized portion of the selected food item.

Participants were included in our final sample according to the following criteria: (1) 100% performance on instruction comprehension, AI-screening, and attention checks; (2) full experiment completion with valid responses for at least 80% of trials; and finally (3) overall performance significantly above chance (one-sided binomial test, p < 0.05).
A significant main effect of memorability bin indicates that participants are more likely to choose more memorable old cards regardless of their value (consistent with a memorability bias).
Overall memorability × value difference: participants are more sensitive to value differences between memorable cues.
(B) In Experiment 1B, participants had stronger recognition and value recall performance for more memorable cue images.

info.title: Memorable Decision Cues are More Associable With Value

author.affiliation:

text.text: When making decisions, we must use the sensory cues available at the moment of choice to predict the values of our options.
Yet little is known about how properties of these cues affect the choice process, particularly our ability to retrieve decision-relevant memories.
Here, we test whether and how image memorability, the population likelihood of recognizing a particular image, influences memory-guided decisions.
Across five pre-registered experiments, memorable cue images were not chosen more overall; instead, they predicted more accurate retrieval of associated values and more value-sensitive choices.
We account for this pattern of behavior with a formal exemplar model in which distinctive cues suffer less interference from competing memories during retrieval of associated values.

The model predicts, and our data confirm, two interactions: choices are more sensitive to value differences between memorable options, and a difference in memorability biases choices toward the more memorable option when both are high in value, but away from it when both are low.

Finally, we find that the same pattern held for choices between common foods, suggesting that shared associative memory processes are recruited for choices involving both novel and highly familiar options.
Together, our results suggest that more memorable cues are more associable with value, and provide a process-level account for how memorability influences downstream decisions.
When confronted with a decision, we have rich memory traces for past experiences that we can use to predict the outcome of choice options.
However, at the time of choice, we only have access to current sensory cues, such as a candy wrapper or a book cover.
How do we use these cues to make a decision?
One possibility is to base decisions on memory strength, or familiarity, of the cue itself.

For instance, a series of studies on the memory bias demonstrated that people tend to prefer choice options for which they have stronger memories (Gluth et al., 2015; Weilbächer et al., 2020; Kraemer et al., 2022; Mechera-Ostrovsky and Gluth, 2018).

text.text: Similarly, people are more willing to bet on lotteries with more familiar cues, when they need to recall reward probabilities from memory (Vaidya and Badre, 2020; Vaidya et al., 2025).

text.text: Relatedly, classic studies of the "mere exposure" effect showed that greater familiarity (either from life experience or through experimental repetition) can increase the associated value of a stimulus (Zajonc, 1968).
text.formatted: Relatedly, classic studies of the "mere exposure" effect showed that greater familiarity (either from life experience or through experimental repetition) can increase the associated value of a stimulus <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">(Zajonc, 1968)</ref>.

text.text: And finally, to the extent that people spend more time looking at more memorable stimuli (Dubey et al., 2015; Sulewski et al., 2026; Chakravarthula et al., 2025) and looking time predicts preferential choice (Shimojo et al., 2003; Armel et al., 2008; Krajbich et al., 2010), we would expect a choice bias towards memorable cues, at least in choices between appetitive options (Armel et al., 2008).
text.formatted: And finally, to the extent that people spend more time looking at more memorable stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Dubey et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Sulewski et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Chakravarthula et al., 2025)</ref> and looking time predicts preferential choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Shimojo et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Armel et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Krajbich et al., 2010)</ref>, we would expect a choice bias towards memorable cues, at least in choices between appetitive options <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Armel et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Another possibility is to recruit associative memory processes to recall value information associated with a decision cue.

This putative role for associative or relational memory (Weber et al., 1995; Madan et al., 2014; Shohamy and Daw, 2015; Murty et al., 2016; Wimmer and Büchel, 2016; Duncan and Shohamy, 2016; Bornstein et al., 2017; Bakkour et al., 2019) suggests that our choices are in part determined by how effectively the perceptual presentation of a choice option can be used to access information from memory.

text.text: In a related line of work, Gomilsek et al. (2025) demonstrated that repeated presentation of cue-value pairs, rather than instill an overall familiarity bias, makes subsequent choices more sensitive to associated values, consistent with stronger associative retrieval.

text.text: While much research has investigated value-based choice, far less is known about how properties of a cue affect our ability to retrieve and use value information associated with it.

text.text: If memorable cues are indeed more associable, one underlying reason may be related to their distinctiveness: distinctive stimuli tend to be both better recognized and serve as stronger cues for associative recall (Going and Read, 1974; Busey and Tunnicliff, 1999; Konkle et al., 2010; Lockhead, 1970; Bruyer and Courvoisier, 1990; Pantelis et al., 2008).

text.text: Here, we ask: how does the memorability of decision cues influence value-based choices?
One possibility is that memorable cues will be chosen more overall, a memorability bias.
Alternatively, more memorable images may be more associable with value, supporting stronger retrieval of values from memory and more value-sensitive choices.
2  Across five pre-registered behavioral experiments, we demonstrate strong support for the latter, that more memorable decision cues predict better retrieval of associated value to guide decisions.
In Experiment 1A, we find that memory-guided choices are more sensitive to associated values for more memorable cues.
In Experiment 1B, we separate recognition memory from value recall and find that memorability affects both.
These results suggest that more memorable cues are more associable with value, and that the properties of a cue affect how associated information is retrieved.

We show that our data are naturally explained by an exemplar model of memory, in which cue distinctiveness mitigates interference and thus produces both greater recognition performance and more accurate associative recall.
From this formal account, we derive two novel predictions about how memorability and value interact to shape choices.

In Experiments 2A and 2B, we confirm these predictions empirically; choices are more sensitive to differences in value when cues are more memorable, and the effect of cue memorability differs as a function of the value of choice options, rather than leading to a simple bias towards the more memorable cue.
Finally, we test whether the same principles apply to food choices (Armel et al., 2008; Hare et al., 2009; Steinglass et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Finally, we test whether the same principles apply to food choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Armel et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Hare et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Steinglass et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike the previous experiments, which explicitly rely on single episodic memories, food choices are putatively based on preferences learned over a lifetime of experiences, cued with highly familiar stimuli.
Surprisingly, even here, we find that memorability similarly modulates the retrieval of value associations to guide choices, consistent with the predictions of our exemplar-model account.

Together, our findings suggest that image memorability has cascading consequences for associative memory of value and decision-making, both for novel and highly familiar choice options, and provide a formal, process-level account of how memorability influences value-based decisions.
All results presented follow from preregistered analyses, unless noted as exploratory (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/Z9Y5F).

text.text: We then turn to our primary question of interest: how does the memorability of a card's image influence these memory-guided choices?
One possibility is an overall memorability bias: that more memorable cards are inferred to be higher value, and thus chosen more overall.

Alternatively, if more memorable cards are more associable with their learned values, choices will be more sensitive to the values of higher memorability cards, predicting an interaction between value and memorability on choices.

These data reveal an interaction between memorability and value, where cue memorability supports stronger memory for associated values retrieved at the time of choice.

The results of Experiment 1 demonstrate that the memorability of a cue image predicts more accurate retrieval of associative values and choices that are more sensitive to these retrieved values.

These results are somewhat surprising, in light of decades of work showing theoretical and functional distinctions between item and associative memory (Buchler et al., 2008; Clark and Gronlund, 1996; Raaijmakers and Shiffrin, 1981; Yonelinas, 2002).
text.formatted: These results are somewhat surprising, in light of decades of work showing theoretical and functional distinctions between item and associative memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Buchler et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Clark and Gronlund, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Raaijmakers and Shiffrin, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Yonelinas, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Why, then, would item memorability be related to both associative memory and choice?
The distinctiveness of decision cues offers a possible answer (Murdock Jr., 1960; Schmidt, 1991).
text.formatted: The distinctiveness of decision cues offers a possible answer <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Murdock Jr., 1960;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Schmidt, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Image distinctiveness (in relation to other stored memories) is known to facilitate recognition memory (Going and Read, 1974; Busey and Tunnicliff, 1999; Konkle et al., 2010), as well as associative recall (Lockhead, 1970; Bruyer and Courvoisier, 1990; Pantelis et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Image distinctiveness (in relation to other stored memories) is known to facilitate recognition memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Going and Read, 1974;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Busey and Tunnicliff, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Konkle et al., 2010)</ref>, as well as associative recall <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Lockhead, 1970;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Bruyer and Courvoisier, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Pantelis et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, several studies have related image memorability to various measures of distinctiveness (Lukavský and Děchtěrenko, 2017; Bylinskii et al., 2015; Bainbridge et al., 2013; Valentine et al., 2016), and most recently Simpson et al. (2026) showed that image memorability is highly correlated with several measures of distinctiveness in the (THINGSmem Kramer et al., 2023) dataset, from which our stimuli are drawn.

(2026)</ref> showed that image memorability is highly correlated with several measures of distinctiveness in the (THINGSmem <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Kramer et al., 2023)</ref> dataset, from which our stimuli are drawn.

text.text: How, mechanistically, could cue distinctiveness give rise to the pattern of results in Experiment 1?
Exemplar (or instance) models provide a process-level framework to understand these phenomena (Hintzman, 1984; Nosofsky, 1988).
text.formatted: Exemplar (or instance) models provide a process-level framework to understand these phenomena <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Hintzman, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Nosofsky, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: In these models, each experience is stored as a separate memory trace, and during retrieval, each trace is activated according to its similarity to the cue.

Recognition judgments can then be computed on the summed activation ("global match") (Hintzman, 1984; Nosofsky, 1988), and reconstructed stimuli, category labels, or other associated information (such as reward) can be predicted with averages in which each memory trace is weighted by its activation (DeLosh et al., 1997; Medin and Schaffer, 1978; Nosofsky, 1986).
text.formatted: Recognition judgments can then be computed on the summed activation ("global match") <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Hintzman, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Nosofsky, 1988)</ref>, and reconstructed stimuli, category labels, or other associated information (such as reward) can be predicted with averages in which each memory trace is weighted by its activation <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(DeLosh et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Medin and Schaffer, 1978;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Nosofsky, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: Distinctive cues produce less interference from competing memories, and therefore more accurate memory retrieval.

Indeed, recent work has used exemplar models of image distinctiveness to explain image memorability, explaining as much variance as image-based deep learning approaches (Meagher and Nosofsky, 2023; Nosofsky et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Indeed, recent work has used exemplar models of image distinctiveness to explain image memorability, explaining as much variance as image-based deep learning approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Meagher and Nosofsky, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Nosofsky et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Qualitatively, Nairne (2002) also pointed out that these models predict that distinctive images will be better for retrieving a target paired associate.
text.formatted: Qualitatively, <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Nairne (2002)</ref> also pointed out that these models predict that distinctive images will be better for retrieving a target paired associate.

text.text: However, we are currently unaware of work relating cue distinctiveness and choice. 4 Here, building on simple exemplar models of choice (Juslin and Persson, 2002; Gomilsek et al., 2025), we introduce a process-level theory for how image memorability (distinctiveness) is related to associative value recall and downstream choice.
text.formatted: However, we are currently unaware of work relating cue distinctiveness and choice. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_3">4</ref> Here, building on simple exemplar models of choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Juslin and Persson, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Gomilsek et al., 2025)</ref>, we introduce a process-level theory for how image memorability (distinctiveness) is related to associative value recall and downstream choice.

text.text: We show that this model accounts of the results of Experiment 1, and we ask what novel predictions this model offers for downstream decision-making.
Our mathematical model (Appendix: Modeling) describes how cue memorability predicts stronger associative recall and more value-sensitive choices, offering two key contributions.
First, we synthesize the ideas above by formalizing how cue distinctiveness drives stronger associative recall (following Nairne, 2002).
text.formatted: First, we synthesize the ideas above by formalizing how cue distinctiveness drives stronger associative recall (following <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Nairne, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Intuitively, cues that are less distinctive (less memorable) produce more interference when trying to retrieve associated values (Morales-Calva et al., 2025), which pulls retrieved value estimates towards the mean of interfering memories.
text.formatted: Intuitively, cues that are less distinctive (less memorable) produce more interference when trying to retrieve associated values <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Morales-Calva et al., 2025)</ref>, which pulls retrieved value estimates towards the mean of interfering memories.

text.text: Image distinctiveness can therefore account for the results of Experiment 1, where more memorable cues were more associable with value.
Second, we ask what novel predictions this distinctiveness-based account makes for downstream decisions.

By assuming that values used in choices are retrieved in a way that depends on trace activation (following standard exemplar theories of choice, Juslin and Persson, 2002; Gomilsek et al., 2025), we derive two novel and testable predictions about how memorability and value interact to shape choices.
text.formatted: By assuming that values used in choices are retrieved in a way that depends on trace activation (following standard exemplar theories of choice, <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Juslin and Persson, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Gomilsek et al., 2025)</ref>, we derive two novel and testable predictions about how memorability and value interact to shape choices.

text.text: These predictions apply not just to choices guided by single episodic memory traces (as above), but more generally to any preferential choice between familiar options.
In particular, our model predicts: 1.
P1: Overall memorability × value difference: choices are more sensitive to differences in value between more memorable options, as retrieved values will be less distorted by interference.
P2: Memorability difference × overall value: The effect of cue memorability depends on the value of choice options.

When values are similar, this presents as a reflection effect (Weilbächer et al., 2020; Kahneman and Tversky, 1979): participants prefer the more memorable cue when both are high-value and the less memorable cue when both are low-value.
text.formatted: When values are similar, this presents as a reflection effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">(Weilbächer et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Kahneman and Tversky, 1979)</ref>: participants prefer the more memorable cue when both are high-value and the less memorable cue when both are low-value.

text.text: This arises because less memorable cues evoke more interference, and thus their retrieved values are pulled towards the mean value of competing memories.
Less memorable options will therefore seem worse (when high-value), or better (when low-value) than they really are (see Appendix for more details).
Our theory predicts these interactions insofar as choices recruit episodic memory to estimate the value of choice options.
Notably, under this account, memorability does not make a cue more attractive in itself, but rather sharpens retrieval, making the cue's recalled value less biased by competing memory traces.

For the same reason, it predicts no main effect of overall (summed) memorability. 5Altogether, we find that exemplar models provide a natural and mechanistic account of the data from Experiment 1, describing how cue memorability relates to associative recall and downstream decisions.
text.formatted: For the same reason, it predicts no main effect of overall (summed) memorability. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_4">5</ref>Altogether, we find that exemplar models provide a natural and mechanistic account of the data from Experiment 1, describing how cue memorability relates to associative recall and downstream decisions.

text.text: We now proceed to directly test the two predictions above.
The first (P1) is tested in Experiment 2A, by varying the shared memorability of two choice options with a large difference in value.
The second prediction (P2) is tested in Experiment 2B, by evaluating choices between equal-valued items with a large difference in memorability.
Unlike Experiment 1, directly testing these predictions requires choices between two options with associated values.
Thus, in both Experiments 2A and 2B, "old trial" choices included two old options, and to simplify the task design, we only used high-and low-memorability images.
In Experiment 2A, we set out to directly test for an interaction between the overall memorability of choice options and their difference in value (P1).
That is, are choices more sensitive to the difference in value between two options when their overall (shared) memorability is high?
We note that this interaction is supported by the results of Experiment 1, but there participants had to infer the expected value of a novel foil.
In this experiment, old trials involved two previously-chosen cards, both either high-or low-memorability, with counterbalanced value, memorability, and screen location.

We found that indeed, the overall memorability (roughly shared between both images) strongly predicted the probability of choosing the higher value option (β = .14, SE = .05, p < .01), consistent with P1 (Fig. 3A).
text.formatted: We found that indeed, the overall memorability (roughly shared between both images) strongly predicted the probability of choosing the higher value option (β = .14, SE = .05, p < .01), consistent with P1 (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3A</ref>).

text.text: Thus, choices are more sensitive to differences in value for higher-memorability options.
We note that memory-guided choices in this experiment were far from ceiling, and we predict this effect will be weakened when differences in value are so strong as to induce ceiling performance.
In Experiment 2B, we turn to the second predicted interaction (P2), between two images' overall value and their difference in memorability.
That is, when two choice options have similar or even equal values, how does memorability influence which option is preferred?
To address this question, we modified our task design such that each old trial presented one highmemorability card and one low-memorability card.
On half of the trials ("matched-value" trials), these two cards shared the same value (either both $0 or both $1, in equal proportions).
These trials allowed us to evaluate how memorability influenced choices between equally-valued choice options.
Because choices cannot be based on a difference in true associated value, they also offer a clean test of an overall memorability bias.
On the remaining ("mixed-value") trials, one card was worth $0 and one worth $1 (counterbalanced across

We included these trials to ensure participants attempted to retrieve value information from memory, but they are irrelevant to our main analysis of interest.

On matched-value trials, we found a reliable effect of overall (shared) value on the probability of choosing the higher memorability card (β = 0.26, SE = 0.04, p < .001); consistent with P2, participants were more likely to choose the more memorable card when both were $1 and more likely to choose the less memorable card when both were $0 (Fig. 3B).

text.text: Alternatively put, the overall value interacted with the difference in memorability to predict choices.
These results are inconsistent with an overall memorability bias, as choices in low-value trials were biased away from the more memorable option.
Instead, they are consistent with participants having more precise associative memory for the more memorable card, and choices being more strongly driven by the value of that item.

Together, the results of Experiments 2 confirm two hypothesized interactions between memorability and value on binary choices: between the overall memorability and the difference in value (P1), and between the overall value and the difference in memorability (P2).
The data are consistent with more memorable cue images producing less interference and therefore more precise associative memory for value, rather than an overall memorability bias.
The experiments above evaluate how memorability affects cue-reward associations learned from a single episode within an experimental session.

We then sought to test how these findings generalize to more naturalistic decisions, where choices frequently involve highly familiar options, with preferences learned over a lifetime of reward experiences, and the particular perceptual cues may vary from one encounter to another.
Food choice offers a natural and well-established paradigm for investigating these questions: most people have extensive experience with common foods and make choices between them daily.
It is not obvious that episodic memory (and therefore, memorability, a measure derived from episodic recognition experiments) would influence these choices at all.
However, recent fMRI and patient studies suggest that episodic memory mechanisms underlie deliberation in the context of decisions about food (Bakkour et al., 2019).
text.formatted: However, recent fMRI and patient studies suggest that episodic memory mechanisms underlie deliberation in the context of decisions about food <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bakkour et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: If valuerelated evidence from memory is retrieved to guide food choices, then the memorability of cue images during a decision would be expected to modulate choices.

We conducted an initial test of these predictions by re-analyzing a previously-collected dataset (Li et al., 2022), in which 44 participants performed recognition memory and binary food choice tasks with a standardized set of food images (Lloyd et al., 2020; Armel et al., 2008).

text.text: In their initial analysis, Li et al. (2022) reported no evidence for an overall memorability bias, consistent with our theoretical and empirical results above; participants were not more likely, overall, to choose foods cued with more memorable images.

(2022)</ref> reported no evidence for an overall memorability bias, consistent with our theoretical and empirical results above; participants were not more likely, overall, to choose foods cued with more memorable images.

text.text: This result held even on a subset of trials pairing two foods for which a participant gave similar preference ratings.

Building on this result and our findings from the reward learning experiments, we turned to investigate whether their data support the two interactions predicted by the distinctiveness-based theory presented above (see Appendix: Modeling).
We first analyzed data from the similar-rating trials (analogous to our matched-value trials in Experiment 2B).

We fit a model predicting whether the food option on the right side was chosen, as a function of the signed difference in memorability (right minus left) and their overall value (the sum of their normalized preference ratings).
As our theory predicts (P2), we found a significant interaction between these two variables (β = .54, SE = .24, p = .02) (Fig. S3C).

We next turned to the interaction between overall memorability and value difference: did participants make more value-sensitive choices when the overall memorability is higher (P1)?
We analyzed distantrating trials, where foods were paired with relatively large differences in preference ratings.
We fit a model that included both hypothesized interactions (including both was necessary, as their design did not intentionally include similar-memorability trials as in our Exp.

While choices were sensitive to the difference in value between options (β = 1.25, SE = .09, p < .001), we did not find reliable evidence for the interaction between the difference in value and overall memorability (p = .3).

Why might this interaction not have been present in Li et al. (2022)'s data?
text.formatted: Why might this interaction not have been present in <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Li et al. (2022)</ref>'s data?

text.text: We hypothesized that, because the stimulus pairings ignored memorability in their task, trials did not vary enough in their overall memorability to support this analysis.

Moreover, analyzing only a subset of trials in their 44-person sample may not be sufficiently powered to detect such an interaction, especially in trials where we expect most of the choice variability to be driven by strong value preferences (independent of the cues).

Therefore, we conducted a preregistered follow-up study, with the same design and stimuli, and two changes: (1) we divided up the food images into three equally-sized memorability bins, and only used food options from the highest and lowest bin; and (2) in constructing the distant-rating trials, we ensured that both choice options were in the same bin, ensuring greater variability in overall memorability with relatively small differences in memorability between the options.
We first sought to replicate the interaction between overall value and the difference in memorability (P2).

Across all trials in the experiment, we found a reliable interaction (β = .65, SE = .14, p < .001); the same was true for a model fit to just the subset of similar-rating trials, where we expected this effect to be clearest (β = .82, SE = .17, p < .001; Fig. 4C).

Across all trials, we found a reliable interaction (β = .07, SE = .03, p = .04; Fig. 4B).

On these trials, we did find a large effect of the difference in value rating (β = 1.74, SE = .08, p < .001), consistent with value-sensitive choices.

Thus, we find evidence for both predicted interactions between memorability and value on food choices, with stronger support for P2 than P1.
Decisions about value require inferring the value of choice options from past experience, using only the sensory cues available to us at the time of choice.
In the present work, we investigated how the memorability of decision cues affects retrieval of associated values from memory to guide decisions.

We tested two alternative accounts: first, that memorable images would be preferred more overall (memorability bias), or second, that memorable images would be more associable with value, and thus predict stronger associative retrieval of value and more value-sensitive choices.
Across our pre-registered behavioral experiments, we find strong support for the latter.
In Experiment 1A, we found that decisions based on episodic memories for value were more accurate when cued with more memorable images.
In Experiment 1B, we confirmed that this effect exists separately from image recognition, with stronger direct value recall for more memorable images.
These results extend and support recent demonstrations that image memorability has cascading effects on downstream associative and relational memory.

A recent study of working memory found that image memorability predicted stronger performance for associations, spatial locations, and temporal order (Cheng et al., 2026); another study similarly found stronger spatial source memory judgments but no benefit for temporal source memory (Trinkl and Wolfe, 2025).
text.formatted: A recent study of working memory found that image memorability predicted stronger performance for associations, spatial locations, and temporal order <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Cheng et al., 2026)</ref>; another study similarly found stronger spatial source memory judgments but no benefit for temporal source memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">(Trinkl and Wolfe, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Another recent study found evidence that memorable images were better associated with paired words, even after multi-day delays, and especially for semanticallyunrelated pairs (Wang et al., 2025), while another found evidence that more memorable faces were better cues for associated names but more memorable scenes were not (Cook and Westerman, 2026).
