text.text: These findings raise many questions about underlying mechanisms and relationships between item and associative memory.

If image memorability can be read out from firing patterns in high-level visual cortex (Jaegle et al., 2019; Rust and Mehrpour, 2020; Bainbridge et al., 2017; Lahner et al., 2024), how do these representational properties affect associative memory in the hippocampus and other downstream areas?
text.formatted: If image memorability can be read out from firing patterns in high-level visual cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Jaegle et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Rust and Mehrpour, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bainbridge et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Lahner et al., 2024)</ref>, how do these representational properties affect associative memory in the hippocampus and other downstream areas?

text.text: To begin answering these questions, we propose a mechanistic cognitive model of how cue memorability supports more precise associative retrieval of value.

We draw on classic exemplar models of memory (Hintzman, 1984; Nosofsky, 1988), including recent attempts to capture image-level variation in memorability (Meagher and Nosofsky, 2023; Nosofsky et al., 2025), as well as more recent applications to judgment and decision making (Juslin and Persson, 2002; Gomilsek et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We draw on classic exemplar models of memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Hintzman, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Nosofsky, 1988)</ref>, including recent attempts to capture image-level variation in memorability <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Meagher and Nosofsky, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Nosofsky et al., 2025)</ref>, as well as more recent applications to judgment and decision making <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Juslin and Persson, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Gomilsek et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Our theory rests on the assumptions that (1) a similarity-based process over cues determines how associated values are retrieved, and (2) memorable cues are more distinctive, and thus more resistant to interference from competing memory traces.
Memorable cues naturally yield more accurate estimates of associated values, and the associated values of less memorable cues are pushed towards the mean expected value.

We note that the relationship between memorability and distinctiveness is still a topic of active research; some studies suggest the two are empirically distinct (Kraemer and Gluth, 2023; Bylinskii et al., 2015; Roberts and Bainbridge, 2026), whereas others suggest that the two are theoretically identical and that empirical mismatches come from an inability to properly characterize distinctiveness in the representational space in which memory retrieval operates (Simpson et al., 2026).
text.formatted: We note that the relationship between memorability and distinctiveness is still a topic of active research; some studies suggest the two are empirically distinct <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Kraemer and Gluth, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Bylinskii et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Roberts and Bainbridge, 2026)</ref>, whereas others suggest that the two are theoretically identical and that empirical mismatches come from an inability to properly characterize distinctiveness in the representational space in which memory retrieval operates <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Simpson et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: We also note associability, by triggering retrieval of related information, could itself make items more distinctive (or memorable) in memory.
Future work is necessary to clarify these relationships and the extent to which distinctiveness accounts can fully explain image memorability.

When these value estimates are used to guide choices, this model predicts two key interactions between memorability and value on choice: first, between the overall (summed) memorability and the difference in value between options, and second, between the overall (summed) value and the difference in memorability.
We test these two predictions in Experiment 2.
In Experiment 2A, we find the former: choices are more sensitive to the difference in value between more memorable options.

In Experiment 2B, we find the latter: choices are biased towards the more memorable item when both are high-value and away from the more memorable item when both are low-value, consistent with more precise retrieval of the more memorable item's value.
Together, these results confirm the presence of these two distinct interactions between memorability and value during decisions.

We also note that these effects mirror those in Gomilsek et al. (2025), where cue-value pairs are repeated to strengthen associative memory, although in our experiments these effects arise from cue manipulations alone.
text.formatted: We also note that these effects mirror those in <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Gomilsek et al. (2025)</ref>, where cue-value pairs are repeated to strengthen associative memory, although in our experiments these effects arise from cue manipulations alone.

text.text: Our distinctiveness-based theory provides a parsimonious account of the observed relationships between item memorability on item recognition, cued associative recall, and value-based decisions.

We emphasize that this account does not depend on distinctiveness explaining all of the variability in item memorability, but rather that whatever component of memorability is explained by distinctiveness may drive the relationship between recognition, recall, and choice.
We also highlight that we refer to "distinctiveness" as distinctiveness in memory, which may not be well captured by particular perceptual or conceptual measures.
However, we note that alternative (and potentially related) accounts may also predict the observed effects of memorability on value-based decisions.

For instance, a popular alternative account of what makes stimuli memorable is that they are processed more efficiently ( (Broers et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2024; Bainbridge et al., 2026) but see Sheffi and Makovski, 2026).
text.formatted: For instance, a popular alternative account of what makes stimuli memorable is that they are processed more efficiently ( <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Broers et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Deng et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bainbridge et al., 2026)</ref> but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Sheffi and Makovski, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Although to our knowledge no mechanistic account of this idea yet exists, it is plausible that memorable cues will also produce more efficient associative recall.
In the driftdiffusion model for preferential choice (Milosavljevic et al., 2010), faster processing implies that value-related evidence for a choice option is accumulated at a faster rate.
text.formatted: In the driftdiffusion model for preferential choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Milosavljevic et al., 2010)</ref>, faster processing implies that value-related evidence for a choice option is accumulated at a faster rate.

text.text: In Appendix: An alternate model, we show that the same predicted interactions between memorability and value can be derived under the assumptions that (1) more memorable cues increase the rate of evidence accumulation for associated values, and (2) values are coded relative to a reference point at the average value within an experimentfoot_6 While these assumptions are not as well mechanistically motivated as our distinctiveness-based account, they permit a theoretical link to the large literature on evidence accumulation models of preferential choice (Milosavljevic et al., 2010; Aschenbrenner et al., 1984; Diederich, 1997; Busemeyer, 1985; Busemeyer and Townsend, 1993).
text.formatted: In Appendix: An alternate model, we show that the same predicted interactions between memorability and value can be derived under the assumptions that (1) more memorable cues increase the rate of evidence accumulation for associated values, and (2) values are coded relative to a reference point at the average value within an experiment<ref type="foot" target="#foot_6">foot_6</ref> While these assumptions are not as well mechanistically motivated as our distinctiveness-based account, they permit a theoretical link to the large literature on evidence accumulation models of preferential choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Milosavljevic et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Aschenbrenner et al., 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Diederich, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Busemeyer, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Busemeyer and Townsend, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, memorability in our experiments functions similarly to value certainty (see, in particular, model 5 Lee and Usher, 2023) and attention (Krajbich et al., 2010; Smith and Krajbich, 2019) in other accounts of evidence accumulation in preferential choice.
text.formatted: Indeed, memorability in our experiments functions similarly to value certainty (see, in particular, model 5 Lee and Usher, 2023) and attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Krajbich et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Smith and Krajbich, 2019)</ref> in other accounts of evidence accumulation in preferential choice.

text.text: Cue memorability may even in part underlie the observed patterns of eye movements and subjective feelings of confidence in those settings (Sulewski et al., 2026; Broers and Busch, 2021).
text.formatted: Cue memorability may even in part underlie the observed patterns of eye movements and subjective feelings of confidence in those settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">(Sulewski et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Broers and Busch, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: We also note that our distinctiveness-based account may be in principle compatible with this evidence-accumulation-based account, under additional assumptions about how exemplar retrieval unfolds over time to provide decision evidence.
We hope that future work will further explore all these connections.
We then generalize our account to a more naturalistic domain: preferential food choices.
In food choices, the role of explicit episodic memory retrieval is less obvious, as cues are highly familiar and values may be easily accessible after a lifetime of experiences.

Still, in situations of decision deliberation, recent work has suggested that food choices recruit the same underlying associative and relational memory mechanisms, putatively to retrieve and construct value preferences (Shadlen and Shohamy, 2016; Bakkour et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Still, in situations of decision deliberation, recent work has suggested that food choices recruit the same underlying associative and relational memory mechanisms, putatively to retrieve and construct value preferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Shadlen and Shohamy, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bakkour et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, a recent study reported no overall bias towards preferring foods cued with more memorable images (Li et al., 2022), a finding that we replicate here.
text.formatted: However, a recent study reported no overall bias towards preferring foods cued with more memorable images <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Li et al., 2022)</ref>, a finding that we replicate here.

text.text: Consistent with our theoretical account and the results of the simpler reward learning tasks, we find that cue memorability and value interact to predict food choices.
In particular, when differences in value are small, choices are preferentially sensitive to the associated value of a more memorable cue (mirroring the results of Experiment 2B).

This result, replicated in both published and newly-collected data, suggests that even with familiar choice options like common foods, episodic and associative memory processes (as described by our exemplar model) are recruited to construct preferences during deliberation (Bakkour et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This result, replicated in both published and newly-collected data, suggests that even with familiar choice options like common foods, episodic and associative memory processes (as described by our exemplar model) are recruited to construct preferences during deliberation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bakkour et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We also find that choices are more sensitive to value preferences when food image cues are more memorable, although this effect is considerably smaller and less reliable than the previous.
One possibility is that when choice options differ more strongly in value, other (non-episodic) decision signals are more available.
Multiple learning and decision systems contribute to value-based choices (Doll et al., 2015), and decision signals from the striatum or elsewhere may be more reliably recruited on easier decisions.
text.formatted: Multiple learning and decision systems contribute to value-based choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Doll et al., 2015)</ref>, and decision signals from the striatum or elsewhere may be more reliably recruited on easier decisions.

text.text: On this account, episodic memory may be most valuable under conditions of extensive deliberation, when other sources of evidence do not discriminate between the choice options (as in the "similar-rating" trials).
A related study indeed observed greater hippocampal activation during the (food) decisions with the longest response times-presumably those requiring the most deliberation (Bakkour et al., 2019).
text.formatted: A related study indeed observed greater hippocampal activation during the (food) decisions with the longest response times-presumably those requiring the most deliberation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bakkour et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Still, across all these settings, our results provide strong evidence that shared episodic memory computations underlie both episodic associative retrieval and food choices.
We note that inferring values from cues may recruit alternate behavioral strategies in different settings.
For instance, unlike in the random cue-value pairings used in our tasks, sometimes the perceptual content of a cue itself directly predicts reward outcomes (Gershman and Niv, 2010; Niv et al., 2015).
text.formatted: For instance, unlike in the random cue-value pairings used in our tasks, sometimes the perceptual content of a cue itself directly predicts reward outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Gershman and Niv, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Niv et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In these cases, cue-target similarity can promote adaptive decision-making via generalization (Guttman and Kalish, 1956).
text.formatted: In these cases, cue-target similarity can promote adaptive decision-making via generalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Guttman and Kalish, 1956)</ref>.

text.text: In other cases, cues may contain rich semantic knowledge about the kind of predicted rewards, enabling rapid associations to be formed (Seligman, 1970).
text.formatted: In other cases, cues may contain rich semantic knowledge about the kind of predicted rewards, enabling rapid associations to be formed <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Seligman, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: We predict, as in food choices, that these choices will demonstrate the same effects insofar as relational and associative memory mechanisms are recruited to construct preferences.
Our work has several shortcomings to address in future research.
First, rewards in our tasks were either small (making correct choices in Experiments 1 and 2 resulted in slightly higher bonuses) or entirely noninstrumental (in Experiment 3).

Second, it is possible that the effects of memorability observed here depend on the content of stimuli (Cook and Westerman, 2026); our experiments here are limited to image sets of objects (THINGSmem Kramer et al., 2023) and standard foods (Li et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Second, it is possible that the effects of memorability observed here depend on the content of stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Cook and Westerman, 2026)</ref>; our experiments here are limited to image sets of objects <ref type="bibr">(THINGSmem Kramer et al., 2023)</ref> and standard foods <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Li et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: It is also unclear whether images that are associable with value are more associable with any arbitrary target stimuli.
Future work should also investigate how these effects of memorability relate to the dynamics of decision-making and participant response times, drawing upon evidence accumulation models.

In addition, future work may investigate how to disentangle memorability from other appetitive features of choice options; recent work using generative AI to make stimuli more or less memorable may be a promising approach (Roberts and Bainbridge, 2026).
text.formatted: In addition, future work may investigate how to disentangle memorability from other appetitive features of choice options; recent work using generative AI to make stimuli more or less memorable may be a promising approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Roberts and Bainbridge, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The present work demonstrates that memorable cues are more associable with value, and lead to more value-sensitive decisions.

We present a formal theory of how cue distinctiveness from other exemplars drives both memorability in recognition experiments and more reliable estimates of associative value in a similarityweighted retrieval process.
This account allows us to both make and confirm key predictions about how memorability and value interact to guide decisions.
All five experiments, including hypotheses, sample sizes, exclusion criteria, and statistical models, were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/Z9Y5F).

text.text: We recruited five independent samples of online participants via Prolific.

Eligibility was restricted to Prolific users residing in the United States who reported English as their first language and had an approval rating of at least 99% on previous Prolific studies across at least 50 previous submissions.
Experiments were programmed in jsPsych (version 8.2.3; (Leeuw et al., 2023)) and completed in a web browser.
text.formatted: Experiments were programmed in jsPsych (version 8.2.3; <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Leeuw et al., 2023)</ref>) and completed in a web browser.

text.text: All participants provided informed consent, and all procedures were approved by the Columbia University Institutional Review Board.
Participants received a base payment at a rate of $12/hour, with a performance-dependent bonus.
We applied preregistered exclusion criteria to each sample (see Inclusion Criteria), with a final sample size of N = 100 participants per experiment.
Stimuli for Experiments 1 and 2 were naturalistic object photographs from the THINGS image database (Hebart et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Stimuli for Experiments 1 and 2 were naturalistic object photographs from the THINGS image database <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Hebart et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We used the THINGS memorability scores of Kramer et al. (2023), which were measured in an independent, large-scale continuous recognition task.
text.formatted: We used the THINGS memorability scores of <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Kramer et al. (2023)</ref>, which were measured in an independent, large-scale continuous recognition task.

text.text: Each image's score is its corrected recognition rate: the proportion of observers who correctly recognized the image on its repeat presentation (hit rate) minus the proportion who falsely reported having seen it on its first presentation (false-alarm rate).

We selected a fixed set of 468 images: for each of the 26 higher-level categories (excluding "insect" which did not have enough images), we selected 6 object concepts in each of 3 memorability bins (low, mid, high) for a total of 156 images per bin.
Selection proceeded in two steps.

First, for each object concept we identified one candidate exemplar image for each bin: its lowest-scoring exemplar (for the low bin), its highest-scoring exemplar (for the high bin), and its exemplar closest to the median memorability score of all THINGS images (0.795; for the mid bin).

Second, we used a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) (Slivkoff and Gallant, 2021) to assign object concepts to category-bin slots, subject to the hard constraints that each category contribute exactly six concepts to each bin and that each concept be used at most once.
text.formatted: Second, we used a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">(Slivkoff and Gallant, 2021)</ref> to assign object concepts to category-bin slots, subject to the hard constraints that each category contribute exactly six concepts to each bin and that each concept be used at most once.

text.text: This procedure ensured that each chosen object concept (e.g., aardvark) appeared only once in the set, and that each higher-level category (e.g., animal) was equally represented across memorability bins, while enforcing maximal distance between the three memorability bins.
In the resulting set, average memorability by bin was: low = 0.550 (0.410-0.692), mid = 0.795 (0.789-0.805), high = 0.952 (0.881-1.000).
Experiment 1 used all three bins (the full 468-image set); Experiment 2 used only the low-and high-memorability bins (312 images).
In Experiment 3, following Li et al. (2022), we used images from the Food Folio stimulus set from the Columbia Center for Eating Disorders (Lloyd et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In Experiment 3, following <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Li et al. (2022)</ref>, we used images from the Food Folio stimulus set from the Columbia Center for Eating Disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Lloyd et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Stimuli for the original study included all 138 images in the Food Folio dataset (Lloyd et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Stimuli for the original study included all 138 images in the Food Folio dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Lloyd et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: To best evaluate our memorability-based hypotheses, we ranked these images using the memorability scores collected in Experiment 1A of Li et al. (2022), and only use the lowest 46 and highest 46 items by memorability score (low mean = 0.332, range -0.025-0.415; high mean = 0.607, range 0.527-0.860).

(2022)</ref>, and only use the lowest 46 and highest 46 items by memorability score (low mean = 0.332, range -0.025-0.415; high mean = 0.607, range 0.527-0.860).

text.text: Our experiments adapted the memory-guided decision-making task of Duncan and Shohamy (2016) (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Our experiments adapted the memory-guided decision-making task of <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Duncan and Shohamy (2016)</ref> (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: On each trial, participants used a computer keyboard to choose between two cards, each depicting a unique image.
Cards were 440x440-pixel squares, rendered fullscreen on a 1060x620-pixel canvas.
Each choice lasted for up to 2 seconds.
The chosen card was highlighted for 1 second and then flipped over to reveal its monetary value (either $0 or $1) for 1.5 seconds, followed by a 0.5-second inter-trial interval.
If no response was made within 2 seconds, a "too slow" message was displayed for 1.5 seconds and a randomly selected card flipped over.
On "new" (encoding) trials, both cards depicted images the participant had not yet seen, and the participant learned the value of the card they chose.

On "old" (retrieval) trials, one card (Experiments 1A and 1B) or both cards (Experiments 2A and 2B) had been chosen on an earlier new trial, and participants could use their memory of the value learned for that card to guide their response.
A given image only appeared once or twice; once a card appeared on an old trial, it never appeared again.
Delays between choosing a card and subsequently seeing it again on an old trial ranged from 7 to 15 trials, and were controlled to be roughly uniform (see Trial Sequencing).
Participants saw 3 interspersed attention check trials, which included a hidden prompt to identify AI agents.
Both attention check failures and AI catch responses resulted in data exclusion.

Trial Sequencing For Experiments 1A, 1B, 2A, and 2B, the trial sequence was fixed in advance in order to precisely balance experimental variables and potential confounds (old/new trial type, memorability bin, delay, and value).
Trial sequences were created with a two-phase MILP process.
Phase 1 determined which trials were old or new, with no more than 8 consecutive trials of the same type, and, for each old trial, which earlier new trial supplied its old card (or cards).
Phase 2 assigned each trial's memorability bin and value, with no more than 3 consecutive trials from the same memorability bin.

Phase 2 also matched the distributions of encoding-retrieval delays and left/right positions exactly across memorability bins and values, so that these potential confounds were orthogonal to our main analyses.
We pre-computed ten independent solved sequences per experiment (Experiment 1B reused Experiment 1A's ten sequences), and each participant was randomly assigned one of these ten sequences.
While memorability bins were fixed by these sequences, the particular images assigned to each trial were randomized for each participant.
In Experiment 1A, we tested whether image memorability produces stronger memory for associated values.
The task consisted of 312 trials, involving all 468 images.
Half of the trials were new, and half were old.
The two images on any given trial were always drawn from the same memorability bin.
On each old trial, the participant saw one previously-chosen card and one novel card (52 old trials per memorability bin, half with a $1 old card and half with $0).
Choices on old trials were labeled "accurate" if a participant chose an old card worth $1 or avoided an old card worth $0 (i.e., chose the novel card).
In the old trials of Experiment 1A, a single choice reflects both recognition of the previously seen image and retrieval of its associated value; Experiment 1B separated these two components.

It thereby tested whether THINGS memorability scores predict recognition in our task at all, since the scores come from an independent task (Kramer et al., 2023) with a different response format and much longer delays.
text.formatted: It thereby tested whether THINGS memorability scores predict recognition in our task at all, since the scores come from an independent task <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Kramer et al., 2023)</ref> with a different response format and much longer delays.

text.text: Experiment 1B reused Experiment 1A's trial sequences and stimulus set exactly; only the old trials changed.

On old trials, participants first had 2 seconds to make a 2-alternative-forced-choice recognition judgment ("which of these two cards have you seen before?"), and received feedback for 0.75 seconds: the chosen card was highlighted green if correct or red if incorrect.

Then, regardless of whether the recognition judgment was correct, the old card was shown alone and participants had 2 seconds to make a 2-alternativeforced-choice value memory report, between $0 and $1.
A 0.75-second feedback screen then indicated the correct value.
This direct report measures associative memory for value separately from the recognition judgment.
New trials were identical to Experiment 1A.

Experiment 2A Experiment 2A tested whether the effect of memorability on value-guided choice holds when participants choose between two previously seen cards, removing any influence of the novel foil.
Each old trial showed two previously chosen cards from the same memorability bin, one worth $1 and one worth $0.
Because both cards were equally familiar and from the same bin, a bias toward more memorable images could not by itself produce a correct choice.
We used only the high-and low-memorability bins, giving 234 trials: 156 new trials (78 high, 78 low) and 78 old trials (39 high, 39 low).
Every card chosen on a new trial reappeared on exactly one old trial.
The sequence design matched delays across memorability bins and values, and counterbalanced whether the $1 or the $0 card had the longer delay.
An accurate choice meant choosing the $1 card.
Experiment 2B Experiment 2B tested how memorability influences choice when the two options' values are equal.
Like Experiment 2A, it used only the high-and low-memorability bins, and each old trial showed two previously chosen cards.
Unlike Experiment 2A, the two cards always came from different bins (one high, one low).
The task consisted of 234 trials: 156 new and 78 old.
Forty of the old trials were matched-value trials, on which both cards were worth $1 (20 trials) or both were worth $0 (20 trials).
Matched-value trials have no normatively correct answer, so we analyzed choices on them for biases related to the memorability of the two images.
The remaining 38 old trials were mixed-value trials, on which one card was worth $1 and the other $0 (19 trials with the high-memorability card worth $1 and 19 with it worth $0).
While mixed-value trials were not the focus of our analyses, they ensured that participants stayed motivated to remember card values.

The sequence design matched delays separately within the matched-and mixed-value trials, so that high-and low-memorability cards had identical delay distributions, and the high-memorability card had the longer delay on exactly half of the trials of each kind.
In Experiment 3, we replicated and adapted the sequential food-choice paradigm of Li et al. (2022) (Fig. 4).
text.formatted: In Experiment 3, we replicated and adapted the sequential food-choice paradigm of <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Li et al. (2022)</ref> (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4</ref>).

text.text: Specifically, we ran a version of their "Experiment 1B", including two phases (Fig. 4).
text.formatted: Specifically, we ran a version of their "Experiment 1B", including two phases (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">4</ref>).

text.text: First, during a self-paced rating phase, participants rated the subjective value of each food item; they were asked to imagine they had to eat the food today and reported on a continuous slider how much they would like to eat a snack-sized portion.

Second, during the choice phase, participants had 3 seconds to choose between two previously-rated food items (using a computer keyboard), imagining they would eat a snack-sized portion of the selected food item.
Responses faster than 300ms or slower than 3s elicited a warning message.
Each trial lasted a fixed 4 seconds, including the response period, a 0.5-second highlight around the chosen item, and a fixation for the rest of the 4-second period.
After the rating phase, the 92 foods were ranked by rating phase responses.
Then, following Li et al. (2022), there were two types of choice trials.
text.formatted: Then, following <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Li et al. (2022)</ref>, there were two types of choice trials.

text.text: Half of trials were similar-value trials, in which foods were paired by adjacent ranks (non-overlapping) to produce 46 similar-value pairs.
Half of trials were distantvalue trials, pairing foods of distant ranks.

Here, we deviated from the procedure of Li et al. (2022) by first binning all images into three equal-sized memorability bins (each containing 46 images), and only using the high-and low-memorability bins.
text.formatted: Here, we deviated from the procedure of <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Li et al. (2022)</ref> by first binning all images into three equal-sized memorability bins (each containing 46 images), and only using the high-and low-memorability bins.

text.text: Then, we separately paired high-and low-memorability foods so that each pair shared a same memorability bin (to match Experiment 2A).
Finally, following the original study's procedure, we paired foods 23 ranks away to produce 46 distant-value pairs, 23 within each memorability bin.
Each food appeared in one pairing for each trial type, resulting in a total of 92 choice trials, with randomly interleaved trial types.

Note that differences in memorability thus arose primarily from similar-value trials, and differences in value arose primarily from distant-value trials; below, we model all trials jointly, and separately by trial type.

Participants were included in our final sample according to the following criteria: (1) 100% performance on instruction comprehension, AI-screening, and attention checks; (2) full experiment completion with valid responses for at least 80% of trials; and finally (3) overall performance significantly above chance (one-sided binomial test, p < 0.05).
text.formatted: Participants were included in our final sample according to the following criteria: (1) 100% performance on instruction comprehension, AI-screening, and attention checks; (2) full experiment completion with valid responses for at least 80% of trials; and finally (3) overall performance significantly above chance (one-sided binomial test, p < 0.05).

text.text: This final criterion ensured participants correctly learned and made choices based on associated values.
In Experiments 1A and 2A, it was applied to all old trial choices; in Experiment 1B, to all recognition and value reports, combined; and in Experiment 2B, to choices on mixed-value trials.

For Experiment 3, this performance criterion was replaced to match the inclusion criteria from Li et al. ( 2022):(1) the probability of choosing the rightmost option was not more than 2 standard deviations from the sample mean, (2) response times were above 300 and below 3000ms on more than half of trials, and (3) a positive (p < 0.05) effect of the difference in reported value between choice options on participants' choices.
text.formatted: For Experiment 3, this performance criterion was replaced to match the inclusion criteria from Li et al. ( <ref type="formula">2022):</ref>(1) the probability of choosing the rightmost option was not more than 2 standard deviations from the sample mean, (2) response times were above 300 and below 3000ms on more than half of trials, and (3) a positive (p < 0.05) effect of the difference in reported value between choice options on participants' choices.

text.text: Note that all performance-based criteria apply only to main effects of value, and are thus orthogonal from our primary analyses of memorability.
These criteria resulted in excluding 116, 25, 92, 130, and 38 participants for Experiments 1A, 1B, 2A, 2B, and 3, respectively, to achieve a sample size of 100 included participants for each.
We modeled all outcomes with generalized linear mixed-effects models using the glmer function of the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2015).
text.formatted: We modeled all outcomes with generalized linear mixed-effects models using the glmer function of the lme4 package in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bates et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: For models that did not converge, we followed the procedure of Bates et al. (2018) to find the maximal converging random-effects structure, using likelihood-ratio tests to select the final model.
text.formatted: For models that did not converge, we followed the procedure of <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bates et al. (2018)</ref> to find the maximal converging random-effects structure, using likelihood-ratio tests to select the final model.

text.text: Value was coded as -1 ($0) or +1 ($1).
When memorability bin had three levels (Experiments 1A and 1B), it was an ordered factor (low < mid < high) with orthogonal polynomial contrasts.
text.formatted: When memorability bin had three levels (Experiments 1A and 1B), it was an ordered factor (low < mid < high) with orthogonal polynomial contrasts.

text.text: When it had two levels (Experiments 2A and 2B), it was coded -1 (low) or +1 (high), which is equivalent to the linear polynomial contrast.
Inference for each hypothesis was based on the Wald z-test p-value for the corresponding fixed-effect coefficient or interaction term, at α = .05, two-tailed.

Experiment 1A We modeled whether the old card was chosen as a function of its value, its memorability bin, and their interaction: where old image and new image identify the old card's and the novel foil's images.
A significant old value × memorability bin interaction indicates that choices are more sensitive to the old card's value when its image is more memorable (consistent with associability).
A significant main effect of memorability bin indicates that participants are more likely to choose more memorable old cards regardless of their value (consistent with a memorability bias).

Experiment 1B We modeled recognition accuracy and value-report accuracy on old trials, each as a function of the old card's value and memorability bin: glmer(correct_recognition ~old_value * memorability_bin + (old_value * memorability_bin | participant_id) + (old_value | old_image) + (1 | new_image), family = binomial) glmer(correct_recall ~old_value * memorability_bin + (old_value * memorability_bin | participant_id) + (old_value | old_image) + (1 | new_image), family = binomial)

An effect of memorability bin on recognition accuracy tests whether memorability scores predict behavior in this task, and an effect on value-report accuracy tests whether memorability predicts associability with value.

Experiment 2A We modeled choice accuracy (choosing the $1 card) as a function of the memorability bin shared by the two cards: where value1 image and value0 image identify the images of the $1 and $0 cards.
Because every image belongs to exactly one memorability bin, we did not include item-level random slopes for memorability.
A significant positive effect of memorability bin indicates more accurate choices when both cards are highly memorable than when both are low in memorability.

Experiment 2B For matched-value trials, we modeled whether the high-memorability card was chosen as a function of the cards' shared value (overall value: +1 if both cards were worth $1, -1 if both were worth $0): glmer(chose_high_mem ~overall_value + (overall_value | participant_id) + (overall_value | high_mem_image) + (overall_value | low_mem_image), family = binomial) A significant positive overall value slope indicates that participants chose the more memorable card when both cards were worth $1 and avoided it when both were worth $0.
A significant intercept indicates an overall bias toward the more memorable card regardless of value.
A significant delta value × overall memorability interaction indicates that choices are more consistent with values when both options are more memorable.

A significant delta memorability × overall value interaction indicates that participants favor the more memorable option when both options are high in value and the less memorable option when both are low.
A main effect of delta memorability indicates an overall bias toward the more memorable option.
We also fit restricted versions of this model to subsets of the data.

For the similar-rating trials, we fit the following model, assuming that the differences in value were approximately zero: glmer(chose_right ~ delta_memorability * overall_value + (delta_memorability * overall_value | participant_id) + (1 | right_image) + (1 | left_image), family = binomial)

We present an account of why image memorability may predict value associability, drawing on mechanistic exemplar models of memory and comparative judgment (Hintzman, 1984; Nosofsky, 1988; Juslin and Persson, 2002; Gomilsek et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We present an account of why image memorability may predict value associability, drawing on mechanistic exemplar models of memory and comparative judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Hintzman, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Nosofsky, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Juslin and Persson, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Gomilsek et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Our account rests on three assumptions: (1) the value of a cue is recalled by retrieving similar exemplars from memory, (2) more memorable cues are more distinctive, and thus face less interference from other exemplars, and (3) choices are based on the recalled values.
Our approach follows that of Gomilsek et al. (2025), who, in their "recollection-based model", use similar principles to show how cue-value repetition affects value-based decisionsfoot_7 .

text.text: Our experiments, in contrast, manipulate only the properties of the cue, and thus we extend their model to explain how cue memorability can influence the downstream recall and choice processes.
Together, this model yields natural predictions about interactions between memorability and value that we describe below and confirm directly in Experiments 2 and 3.
Value recall.

We assume that, when a participant is in the experiment, they store the J stimuli they have seen previously in their memory, each associated with a value v j (in our Experiments 1 and 2, v j ∈ {0, 1}).
On an old trial, cue i appears, and the participant then estimates its value v i by retrieving exemplars in proportion to their similarity, s ij , computed on the cues' non-value features.
Value recall therefore proceeds through a cue-matching process, and the value estimate is the similarity-weighted average (
In Gomilsek et al. (2025), cues were presented repeatedly, with each repetition adding another exemplar with maximal similarity to the cue.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Gomilsek et al. (2025)</ref>, cues were presented repeatedly, with each repetition adding another exemplar with maximal similarity to the cue.

text.text: Value retrieval then naturally becomes more accurate as this matching process becomes dominated by signal from repeated trials of the same cue-value pair.
In our experiments, however, each cue is seen only once, so repetition cannot drive differences in recall accuracy.
Instead, what matters is how much the cue's single trace competes with traces of other cues.

Recent work has argued that more memorable stimuli are more distinctive (in the representational space in which memory storage and retrieval occurs) (Simpson et al., 2026; Morales-Calva et al., 2025).

text.text: For our purposes, however, this simply means that particularly memorable stimuli will be even less similar to other stored exemplars (choice options).
Indeed, Simpson et al. (2026) showed that memorability is strongly correlated with a measure of distinctiveness in the THINGSmem dataset (Kramer et al., 2023), from which our stimuli are drawn.

text.text: Thus, more memorable stimuli will have lower similarity to other choice options presented in the experiment, leading to the weighted sum being dominated by the true associated value for probe i rather than interference from other stimuli.

This is similar to the recall benefits of distinctive cues seen in related models such as the search of associative memory (SAM) model (Gillund and Shiffrin, 1984; Raaijmakers and Shiffrin, 1981) and the model of Nairne (2002).

We note that this distinctiveness D i corresponds (inversely) to Shepard's probability P i of confusing stimulus i with another stimulus (Shepard, 1957), or equivalently to the probability of accurately reconstructing i given itself as a probe.

Following Gomilsek et al. text.text: This motivates using logistic regression to fit our choice data as a function of values, as is standard in the decision-making literature.
However, because we observe only the true values (not the recalled values), we decompose this further using the recall model from above:
We define δ D = D o -D p as the difference in distinctiveness and Σ D = D o +D p as the summed distinctiveness; δ v and Σ v are the corresponding terms for value.
Since D o = (Σ D + δ D )/2 and D p = (Σ D -δ D )/2, the first part of the equation becomes
Including the last term (-δ D V µ ), we get

Term (a) says that sensitivity to the value difference grows with the pair's overall distinctiveness: when both cues are distinctive, their recalled values are close to their true values, and the better option is chosen more reliably.
Term (b) says that a difference in distinctiveness biases choice in a direction that depends on the pair's overall value.

Because the more distinctive cue is shrunk less toward the mean, it is recalled as better than its counterpart when both cues are above the mean (Σ v > 2V µ ) and as worse when both are below it (Σ v < 2V µ ).

text.text: When Σ v = 2V µ , overall distinctiveness has no effect.
Finally, substituting this decomposition into the choice rule, we get
This is a logistic regression in which the effect of value difference depends on overall memorability (distinctiveness), and the effect of memorability difference depends on overall value.
It yields two key predictions: 1.
Overall memorability × value difference: participants are more sensitive to value differences between memorable cues.
Memorability difference × overall value: participants prefer the more memorable cue when both cues are high in value and the less memorable cue when both are low in value.
The first prediction is directly tested in Experiment 2A, by varying the summed memorability of two choice options with distinct values.
The second prediction is directly tested in Experiment 2B, by evaluating choices between equal-valued items with a large difference in memorability.

With binary values (V µ = .5), Σ v -2V µ takes the values +1, 0, and -1, so the model predicts a "reflection effect": memorable cues are preferred in high-high pairs, avoided in low-low pairs, and memorability difference has no effect in mixed pairs.
We also test for both interactions in Experiment 3.
In Experiment 1, where old trials only involve one old option, we assume that participants infer the novel card's value to be the mean over the experiment ($0.50).

Notably, the model predicts no main effect of memorability difference, because memorability does not make a cue more attractive in itself; it only sharpens retrieval, making the cue's recalled value less biased by competitors.
For the same reason, it predicts no main effect of overall memorability.

Lastly, we note that the relationship between memorability and distinctiveness is still an active area of research (Simpson et al., 2026; Roberts and Bainbridge, 2026; Nosofsky et al., 2025; Bainbridge, 2026; Bylinskii et al., 2015).

text.text: We refer to distinctiveness here as it functions in the representational space in which memories are stored and retrieved (which is unknown), but this concept deserves more consideration in future experimental work.
An alternate model of memorability as processing efficiency.
The distinctiveness-based account above provides a parsimonious explanation for the effects of memorability on choices in our data.
How, though, does this model relate to traditional evidence-accumulation models of decision-making?

Here, we show that under certain assumptions, the same empirical predictions about how choice relates to memorability follow from the idea that memorability enhances processing efficiency in an evidence accumulation process.
Indeed, recent studies suggest that memorable stimuli are processed more quickly ( (Broers et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2024; Bainbridge et al., 2026) but see Sheffi and Makovski, 2026).
text.formatted: Indeed, recent studies suggest that memorable stimuli are processed more quickly ( <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Broers et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Deng et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bainbridge et al., 2026)</ref> but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Sheffi and Makovski, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In the drift-diffusion model for preferential choice (Milosavljevic et al., 2010), faster processing implies that value-related evidence for a choice option is accumulated at a faster rate.

text.text: We show below that this account, that memorability speeds the accumulation of value evidence, predicts the same interactions on binary choices as the distinctiveness account above, and we outline how these alternative accounts may be compatible with each other.
We note that this account is formally very similar to the one used to account for the memory bias (Gluth et al., 2015).

However, to predict the exact effects observed in Experiments 2A and 2B, this account needs one additional assumption: that in our experiment, values are encoded by a participant in a reference-dependent way (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979)-that is, that $0 is experienced as a negative reward (relative to the average reward experienced in the experiments), rather than a lack of reward.

text.text: In contrast, this reference-dependence naturally falls out of the distinctiveness mechanism, in which interference from memory competition pulls value estimates towards the average value of stored exemplars (in our experiments, $0.50).
For this reason, we believe the distinctiveness account presents the most parsimonious account of our data, although under certain assumptions, the two accounts could be compatible.
Namely, the exemplar model lacks any notion of time, as a global match or content echo (Hintzman, 1984) computation is typically assumed to occur in fixed time.

Nevertheless, formulating the effect of memorability in an evidence accumulation framework highlights certain parallels to related research.
